<reason>A won by making the live clash easier to decide: both sides are honor codes for students schools can actually reach, so the instruction is the policy. A showed a permission default asks those students to annotate a generated draft, while a ban still asks them to compose. B’s enforcement, detector, and “preference not to know” points were strong, but they never showed that citation-plus-logs restore blank-page practice or that the motion itself requires failing disclosed outsourcing rather than merely permitting it with receipts. B’s opening clip and post-concession return to “ban is fiction” left A’s authorship weighing cleaner.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A’s second rebuttal (A4.3–A4.6) split “permissible to submit” from a required fail of empty process, then described the ordinary obedient case—generate the argument, tidy a few sentences, log “I checked claims”—as allowed under the motion but writing under a ban.</best_rebuttal>
